blocks.text: **The task.** If any cell of an M x N matrix is 0, set its entire row and column to 0. Do it in place.

The naive approach zeroes a row the moment it finds a 0 — and that is wrong. Those freshly written zeroes are indistinguishable from original ones, so the next pass treats them as triggers and cascades until the whole matrix is zero.
So the work must happen in two phases: **record** first, **apply** second.
Collect the affected rows and columns in two sets, then apply. O(M + N) space:
The follow-up asks for constant space, and the trick echoes the cyclic sort chapter: **store the markers inside the matrix itself.**
Use the first row and first column as the notepad. If `matrix[r][c]` is 0, mark `matrix[r][0]` and `matrix[0][c]`.
`matrix[0][0]` would have to mean two things at once — "row 0 has a zero" and "column 0 has a zero". One cell cannot hold both, so column 0 gets its own boolean and the inner loops start at `c = 1`.
Why the second pass runs backwards

The markers live in row 0 and column 0. Applying forwards would overwrite a marker before the later cells that depend on it are read. Working from the bottom-right inward means every marker is consumed before it is destroyed.
